evidence.locator: line 53 SHA-256 ee7617e3af48cbe20347dba3c1c4d2a268848fe98f4173ca58582115a020159f; primary text: Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Part I, chapter XIII 'Of the Natural Condition of Mankind as concerning their Felicity and Misery' (Project Gutenberg ebook 3207; Fordham Internet History Sourcebook 'Thomas Hobbes: Leviathan, Chaps 13-14, 1651', sourcebooks.web.fordham.edu/mod/hobbes-lev13.asp), consulted 2026-11-07 through web copies of the chapter, not a page-cited printed edition
evidence.explanation: SOURCE WORDING (kept exactly as printed, not corrected): 'Thomas Hobbes referred to as a primitive society. This is a society where life is solitary, poor, wicked and short.' PRIMARY WORDING, recorded here only as verification evidence: the chapter describes the life of man in that condition as 'solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short' (1651 spelling; modern 'poor'). Findings: (a) 'wicked' is not Hobbes's word and 'nasty, brutish' are missing from the source's version, so the source line is not a faithful quotation of Hobbes; (b) 'primitive society' is not Hobbes's term: his chapter is about the natural condition of mankind, a condition with no common power to keep all in awe, which he describes as a war of every man against every man, so teaching it as Hobbes's 'theory of a primitive society' misdescribes the argument; (c) in the same chapter Hobbes illustrates with peoples of America, a seventeenth-century illustration that a lesson must attribute to Hobbes and not state as established fact about any people.

evidence.locator: line 54 SHA-256 4a14a957156422a17a44bfc936d8f186f93bf42ec94febca6b83acee323124c2
evidence.explanation: Line 54 states 'people will have to surrender their natural rights' to government as plain fact. That is the social-contract account associated with Hobbes (and, in different forms, with other contract theorists), and it is a contested position in political thought, not a settled rule. It must be taught as an attributed account with alternatives presented neutrally and no endorsement. The factual replacement is not authored here: it is a delivery replacement per the contract, tracked by GOV-LES-T1-W01-CORRECTED-WEEK and open item GOVERNMENT-T1-W01-HOBBES-CORRECTION.

evidence.explanation: The six categories are taught, but de facto is incorrectly defined as sovereignty acquired through force, while de jure is reduced to acquisition according to domestic law. A vassal was a person in a lord-vassal relationship; a serf was an unfree peasant tenant/worker. They are not synonyms.

coverage.objective: Historical background to colonial administration in West Africa, including the Berlin Conference and partition.
coverage.objective_locator: SSS 1/2nd Term SS1_/GOVT.docx; member SHA-256 bce2ae4a8b26f1737631e99387fed3cba661e328da3df274f673b6850088d782; word/document.xml w:body children 39; Week One children 35–88 C14N SHA-256 491d4a2a7ec077af389fc995ebe43a2d75dfac5d11bd60954f17e946637d31ad; exact anchor "Following the Berlin Conference"

evidence.locator: SSS 1/2nd Term SS1_/GOVT.docx; member SHA-256 bce2ae4a8b26f1737631e99387fed3cba661e328da3df274f673b6850088d782; word/document.xml w:body children 39; Week One children 35–88 C14N SHA-256 491d4a2a7ec077af389fc995ebe43a2d75dfac5d11bd60954f17e946637d31ad; exact anchor "Following the Berlin Conference"
evidence.explanation: The source identifies the Berlin Conference and Bismarck, but overstates the conference as the event that partitioned West Africa, gives an overgeneralized list of colonial powers and gives 1885–1950s as the period of colonial rule. The conference (15 November 1884–26 February 1885) established rules for European territorial claims; it did not draw specific borders. Decolonization in West Africa extended through the 1960s and 1970s.

evidence.locator: SSS 1/2nd Term SS1_/GOVT.docx; member SHA-256 bce2ae4a8b26f1737631e99387fed3cba661e328da3df274f673b6850088d782; word/document.xml w:body children 43–48; Week One children 35–88 C14N SHA-256 491d4a2a7ec077af389fc995ebe43a2d75dfac5d11bd60954f17e946637d31ad; exact anchor "REASONS FOR COLONIALISM"
evidence.explanation: The source lists trade, raw materials, markets, slavery, cultural/religious claims and missionary protection. It dates the Industrial Revolution to the seventeenth century (incorrect; the first Industrial Revolution began in eighteenth-century Britain), says colonialism introduced slavery (slavery and slave trading predated formal colonial administration), and presents the colonial 'civilizing' rationale as fact rather than a colonial justification. These claims require correction and attribution.

evidence.explanation: The basic definition is recognizable, but the source says 'Sir Lord Lugard introduced' the system to Nigeria after success in India and Uganda. Lugard helped develop and apply indirect rule in Northern Nigeria; the system was adapted to local political institutions and was not a single uniform model across Nigeria or unique to Britain.

evidence.explanation: The source lists local authorities, customs, tax collection and appointed warrant chiefs. These are useful introductory features, but it overstates preservation of traditional institutions: colonial authorities also altered and subordinated local institutions to colonial administration. The extent and form varied by region.

evidence.locator: SSS 1/2nd Term SS1_/GOVT.docx; member SHA-256 bce2ae4a8b26f1737631e99387fed3cba661e328da3df274f673b6850088d782; word/document.xml w:body children 61–66; Week One children 35–88 C14N SHA-256 491d4a2a7ec077af389fc995ebe43a2d75dfac5d11bd60954f17e946637d31ad; exact anchor "REASONS FOR THE INTRODUCTION OF THE INDIRECT RULE SYSTEM"
evidence.explanation: The source identifies staff, cost, language and local institutions as factors. The climate/disease explanation is overstated, and the claim that the policy was introduced merely to preserve customs is misleading; it also served colonial administrative and fiscal control. The alleged prior success in India and Uganda requires regional and historical qualification.

coverage.objective: Roles of traditional rulers within indirect rule, including tax collection, local administration and communication with colonial authorities.

evidence.locator: SSS 1/2nd Term SS1_/GOVT.docx; member SHA-256 bce2ae4a8b26f1737631e99387fed3cba661e328da3df274f673b6850088d782; word/document.xml w:body children 68–73; Week One children 35–88 C14N SHA-256 491d4a2a7ec077af389fc995ebe43a2d75dfac5d11bd60954f17e946637d31ad; exact anchor "THE ROLES OF TRADITIONAL RULERS IN THE INDIRECT RULE SYSTEM"
evidence.explanation: The source identifies tax collection, communication, local order and Native Authority administration. It overgeneralizes by saying traditional rulers were members of legislative councils; roles varied by region and period, and not every ruler held such a position. Distinguish Native Authorities from legislative councils.

evidence.locator: SSS 1/2nd Term SS1_/GOVT.docx; member SHA-256 bce2ae4a8b26f1737631e99387fed3cba661e328da3df274f673b6850088d782; word/document.xml w:body children 75–80; Week One children 35–88 C14N SHA-256 491d4a2a7ec077af389fc995ebe43a2d75dfac5d11bd60954f17e946637d31ad; exact anchor "INDIRECT RULE IN NORTHERN NIGERIA"
evidence.explanation: The source points to existing emirate institutions and tax administration, but generalizes across all Northern Nigeria and presents claims about Islam teaching submissiveness and low literacy as causal explanations. These are unsupported stereotypes. Explain variation between emirate and non-emirate communities and the role of colonial administrative choices, local institutions, taxation and resistance without attributing a uniform political attitude to a religion or population.

evidence.explanation: The source discusses the Alaafin of Oyo, limits on royal authority, educated elites, taxation and regional political structures. evidence.explanation: The source describes the British use of appointed warrant chiefs and contrasts Eastern Nigeria with the Northern emirate system. Its claim that there were no traditional political institutions is too broad; Igbo political systems varied, with many decentralized communities and some monarchies/centralized institutions.

evidence.locator: SSS 1/2nd Term SS1_/GOVT.docx; member SHA-256 bce2ae4a8b26f1737631e99387fed3cba661e328da3df274f673b6850088d782; word/document.xml w:body children 105–111; Week Two children 89–148 C14N SHA-256 7e79e0f9de9f1909a853fd09d50ecc80bc09122120fcd4c7029eee926f605782; exact anchor "REASONS FOR THE FAILURE OF THE SYSTEM OF INDIRECT RULE IN EASTERN NIGERIA"
evidence.explanation: The source lists lack of centralized chiefs, warrant-chief appointments, local political organization, taxation and alienation of educated elites. It wrongly treats Christianity as a causal explanation and presents Igbo political systems as uniformly decentralized/gerontocratic. The 1929 Women's War involved multiple grievances, including taxation, warrant chiefs and native courts; it should not be reduced to one cause or used as a simple synonym for the failure of the entire system.

evidence.explanation: The source lists lower administrative cost, use of local authorities and changes to local administration. It overstates preservation of traditions and incorrectly attributes the opposition to twin infanticide by Mary Slessor to the indirect-rule system. Slessor was a missionary in Calabar, not an indirect-rule official; the source's causal claim must be corrected.

These effects varied by region and institution; avoid universal statements and clarify the difference between customary authorities, colonial appointees and formal councils.

evidence.locator: SSS 1/2nd Term SS1_/GOVT.docx; member SHA-256 bce2ae4a8b26f1737631e99387fed3cba661e328da3df274f673b6850088d782; word/document.xml w:body children 127–132; Week Two children 89–148 C14N SHA-256 7e79e0f9de9f1909a853fd09d50ecc80bc09122120fcd4c7029eee926f605782; exact anchor "POSITIVE IMPACTS OF COLONIAL RULE IN WEST AFRICA"
evidence.explanation: The source lists several institutional developments, but overstates colonialism as the sole origin of modern government and political parties. The 1922 Clifford Constitution introduced a limited elective principle in Nigeria; the first elections were in 1923, with restricted representation in Lagos and Calabar. The West African Currency Board was established in 1912 and began issuing currency in 1913; the Bank of British West Africa existed from 1894. The source's 'Colonial Bank in 1917' wording needs clarification. Formal education and civil-service development were uneven and built on existing local institutions and initiatives.

coverage.objective: Claimed negative impacts of colonial rule in West Africa, including economic dependence, cultural/linguistic effects and removal or exile of African leaders.

evidence.locator: SSS 1/2nd Term SS1_/GOVT.docx; member SHA-256 bce2ae4a8b26f1737631e99387fed3cba661e328da3df274f673b6850088d782; word/document.xml w:body children 134–139; Week Two children 89–148 C14N SHA-256 7e79e0f9de9f1909a853fd09d50ecc80bc09122120fcd4c7029eee926f605782; exact anchor "NEGATIVE EFFECTS OF COLONIAL RULE IN WEST AFRICA"
evidence.explanation: The source raises important critiques but makes broad claims about language antagonism and industrial absence. ECOWAS, established in 1975, operates across English, French and Portuguese official languages; colonial language differences are real but do not make regional cooperation inherently antagonistic. The source also misdates Ovonramwen's exile (1897, not 1896) and misstates where Jaja of Opobo died (on the return journey at Tenerife in 1891, not in the West Indies). Distinguish slave-trade history from later colonial deportations.

coverage.objective: Claimed positive impacts of colonial rule, including formal education and exposure to wider ideas.
coverage.objective_locator: SSS 1/2nd Term SS1_/GOVT.docx; member SHA-256 bce2ae4a8b26f1737631e99387fed3cba661e328da3df274f673b6850088d782; word/document.xml w:body children 153–158; Week Three children 149–176 C14N SHA-256 0606f62b70ff5309010f52586899b06c38c949cf46f7eb97f9374f58d6c6e177; exact anchor "ADVANTAGES OF COLONIAL RULE"

evidence.locator: SSS 1/2nd Term SS1_/GOVT.docx; member SHA-256 bce2ae4a8b26f1737631e99387fed3cba661e328da3df274f673b6850088d782; word/document.xml w:body children 153–158; Week Three children 149–176 C14N SHA-256 0606f62b70ff5309010f52586899b06c38c949cf46f7eb97f9374f58d6c6e177; exact anchor "ADVANTAGES OF COLONIAL RULE"
evidence.explanation: The source identifies educational expansion and exposure to new ideas. University College Ibadan was established in 1948 as a college of the University of London and became an independent university in 1962. The source should not imply that colonial rule created education or knowledge from nothing; mission, Islamic and indigenous educational traditions predated or coexisted with colonial institutions.

evidence.explanation: The source identifies colonial cultural hierarchy, rural neglect and economic restructuring. These are important critiques but need attribution and evidence by territory and period; the statement that Africans were 'not ready' for the world economy is paternalistic and ignores precolonial trade and diplomatic networks.

coverage.objective: Comparison of British indirect rule and French colonial policy of assimilation/direct administration.
coverage.objective_locator: SSS 1/2nd Term SS1_/GOVT.docx; member SHA-256 bce2ae4a8b26f1737631e99387fed3cba661e328da3df274f673b6850088d782; word/document.xml w:body children 162; Week Three children 149–176 C14N SHA-256 0606f62b70ff5309010f52586899b06c38c949cf46f7eb97f9374f58d6c6e177; exact anchor "INDIRECT RULE / POLICY OF ASSIMILATION"

evidence.locator: SSS 1/2nd Term SS1_/GOVT.docx; member SHA-256 bce2ae4a8b26f1737631e99387fed3cba661e328da3df274f673b6850088d782; word/document.xml w:body children 162; Week Three children 149–176 C14N SHA-256 0606f62b70ff5309010f52586899b06c38c949cf46f7eb97f9374f58d6c6e177; exact anchor "INDIRECT RULE / POLICY OF ASSIMILATION"
evidence.explanation: The source contrasts British indirect rule with French assimilation/direct rule. The comparison is too binary: French administrations also used chiefs and African intermediaries, while British practice varied and included direct administration in some contexts. Assimilation was an official ideology whose practical application was limited and changed over time; it is not synonymous with every form of direct rule.

evidence.locator: SSS 1/2nd Term SS1_/GOVT.docx; member SHA-256 bce2ae4a8b26f1737631e99387fed3cba661e328da3df274f673b6850088d782; word/document.xml w:body children 162; Week Three children 149–176 C14N SHA-256 0606f62b70ff5309010f52586899b06c38c949cf46f7eb97f9374f58d6c6e177; exact anchor "INDIRECT RULE / POLICY OF ASSIMILATION"; table C14N SHA-256 b63ad595c7d4d7a9a3b0a0b9b8f17c8e

evidence.locator: SSS 1/2nd Term SS1_/GOVT.docx; member SHA-256 bce2ae4a8b26f1737631e99387fed3cba661e328da3df274f673b6850088d782; word/document.xml w:body children 196–203; Week Four children 177–209 C14N SHA-256 d6f82017c91ef3cc580f63e9ad4922478bba1e7db520dd5d8774163571113aac; exact anchor "KEY NATIONALIST LEADERS IN NIGERIA AND THEIR CONTRIBUTIONS TO NATIONALISM"
evidence.explanation: The source includes useful biographical anchors, but has factual and attribution problems: Ahmadu Bello's birth year is 1910, not 1909; Macaulay's NNDP was founded in 1923 and his relationship to the Lagos Daily News is misstated; Azikiwe's West African Pilot began in 1937 and he became NCNC Secretary-General later; Awolowo's exact role in the TUC needs qualification. The separate list also misidentifies Jimi Solanke as a nationalist leader.

coverage.objective: Features, merits and demerits of the Clifford Constitution of 1922.
coverage.objective_locator: SSS 1/2nd Term SS1_/GOVT.docx; member SHA-256 bce2ae4a8b26f1737631e99387fed3cba661e328da3df274f673b6850088d782; word/document.xml w:body children 212–234; Week Five children 210–280 C14N SHA-256 619d2c0a026a20faa291e6bc0a0558cd60729596f1239c81cc97373dc1fdd410; exact anchor "TOPIC: CLIFFORD CONSTITUTION OF 1922"

evidence.locator: SSS 1/2nd Term SS1_/GOVT.docx; member SHA-256 bce2ae4a8b26f1737631e99387fed3cba661e328da3df274f673b6850088d782; word/document.xml w:body children 212–234; Week Five children 210–280 C14N SHA-256 619d2c0a026a20faa291e6bc0a0558cd60729596f1239c81cc97373dc1fdd410; exact anchor "TOPIC: CLIFFORD CONSTITUTION OF 1922"
evidence.explanation: The source covers the Legislative Council, elected seats, franchise, merits and demerits. It misstates the elected-member allocation (three Lagos, one Calabar), overstates the elective principle as first in Africa rather than first in Nigeria, and implies the 1922 constitution created a new executive council when an executive council already existed. The council's legislative jurisdiction was confined to the South; the Governor legislated for the North by proclamation.

evidence.locator: SSS 1/2nd Term SS1_/GOVT.docx; member SHA-256 bce2ae4a8b26f1737631e99387fed3cba661e328da3df274f673b6850088d782; word/document.xml w:body children 236–255; Week Five children 210–280 C14N SHA-256 619d2c0a026a20faa291e6bc0a0558cd60729596f1239c81cc97373dc1fdd410; exact anchor "RICHARDS CONSTITUTION FEATURES"

It must distinguish regional councils (which were not legislative bodies) from the central council, specify the limited Lagos/Calabar elective franchise and £50 income threshold, and distinguish the constitution's stated unity aims from the political effects of regionalism.

open_items.detail: Source line 53 says the society without government is what Thomas Hobbes 'referred to as a primitive society', where life is 'solitary, poor, wicked and short'. Checked against Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Part I, chapter XIII (consulted through web copies on 2026-11-07, not a page-cited edition): Hobbes's wording is 'solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short'; 'wicked' is not his word; 'primitive society' is not his term (he writes of the natural condition of mankind and a war of every man against every man); and his illustration from peoples of America is a seventeenth-century claim, not established fact. Line 54 also states the surrender of natural rights to government as plain fact, which is a contested contract account. The source wording stays as printed in the original lesson; the corrected teaching is a delivery replacement, not an edit of the source.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T1-W01-CORRECTED-WEEK, teach Hobbes's argument attributed to Leviathan Part I ch. XIII in original wording, give any quoted primary wording separately and labelled as Hobbes's (short quotation only), cite a page- or section-level edition with its date, present the social-contract account and its alternatives neutrally with attribution and no endorsement, and add a delivery_corrections entry binding SS1-SRC-40ce7dcaf672:BODY:cbce46f8555ccf042f113c0d5694daeb0e617e2cb7dfdb915fe1c7b939990e04 to the replacement. open_items.detail: Week Two's law feature (getBody lines 113–114) says the body of rules regulating conduct 'is called the constitution'. This conflates laws generally with the constitution. The Constitution is supreme law (s.1) and separately vests legislative powers to enact laws (s.4).
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T1-W02-CORRECTED-WEEK, distinguish law as a system of rules from the constitution as the supreme legal framework; explain that statutes and other valid laws also exist. Cite the applicable constitutional text and preserve the original wording only in source evidence.

open_items.detail: The ten-function list at getBody lines 124–135 mixes constitutional powers, policy objectives and broad textbook descriptions. The Constitution supports the general fields but does not rank law-and-order as universally 'the primary and most important' function. Section 17(3)(a) describes opportunities for suitable employment, not a promise that government directly provides every job. The prison claim needs a correctional-law check.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T1-W02-CORRECTED-WEEK, retain the list as an attributed textbook classification, distinguish powers under ss.4–6 from policy objectives under ss.14–19, qualify employment as an opportunity/policy objective, and verify the prison/correctional-service point against applicable law. Cite dated constitutional sources and do not present a textbook ranking as law.

open_items.detail: Week Two line 144 states: 'The ultimate aim of government is to make us political scientists'. This confuses the educational value of studying Government with the purpose of government. Constitution s.14(2)(b) identifies security and welfare as government's primary purpose; OpenStax describes political science as the systematic study of political phenomena and notes there is no unanimity on government's proper purpose.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T1-W02-CORRECTED-WEEK, distinguish the purpose of studying Government from the purpose of government. Attribute the original line to the source; teach political science as a field of study and cite Constitution s.14(2)(b) for Nigeria's constitutional statement. Present broader political-philosophy positions neutrally.

open_items.detail: The Week Three forms-of-power section conflates constitutional allocation of political powers with electoral selection and describes military power in terms that may imply an unlimited domestic security role.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T1-W03-CORRECTED-WEEK, distinguish constitutional powers of the legislature, executive and judiciary from how elected officeholders are selected. Describe military responsibilities only at a high civic/constitutional level; do not imply blanket policing powers or include operational detail.

open_items.detail: The sources-of-power list overgeneralises inheritance, conflates constitutional power with elections, and labels expert knowledge as 'position of authority'.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, distinguish constitutional allocation from electoral selection; present inheritance as a possible source in hereditary systems rather than a universal rule; and distinguish positional authority from expertise/technical authority. Attribute the textbook taxonomy.

open_items.detail: The source attributes three types to Max Weber but calls them sources of political authority and abbreviates legal-rational authority to 'legal'.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, accurately attribute Weber's three ideal types of legitimate domination/authority as traditional, charismatic and legal-rational, explain them as ideal types, and cite a dated scholarly source.

open_items.detail: The source names Obas, Emirs and Obis as traditional-authority examples without qualifying the diversity and changing legal roles of traditional rulers in Nigeria.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, describe these as examples of traditional titles, not holders of uniform constitutional powers. Use the 2009 APRM Nigeria report only as historical context; verify any current role against the relevant state's current law.

open_items.detail: The source generalises that political power in Africa is derived from military overthrow. Historical research documents coups in some African countries, but describes uneven distribution and distinct waves; it does not support treating coups as the general or normal source of political power across Africa.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, attribute coups as a historical phenomenon in particular countries and periods, not a continent-wide rule or ordinary route to authority. Use dated sources and explain the constitutional norm against unconstitutional changes. Keep discussion high-level and non-operational.

open_items.detail: The source's military-authority category describes a broad right to maintain law and order. Nigeria's Constitution gives the Armed Forces defined responsibilities and separately establishes the Nigeria Police Force; the military does not have an unlimited general policing mandate.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, distinguish the Nigeria Police Force's duties from the Armed Forces' constitutional functions under ss.214 and 217, including limits and conditions in s.217(2)(c). Keep this civic and high-level, with no operational guidance.

open_items.detail: The Week Three reading pointer cites Essential Government (C.C. Dibie), pages 7–8, and Comprehensive Government (J.U. Anyaele), pages 10–11. Exact editions were not supplied or opened.

open_items.detail: The Week Four definition treats legality, popular acceptance and support as interchangeable, and the factors list treats foreign diplomatic acceptance as a direct measure of domestic legitimacy.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T1-W04-CORRECTED-WEEK, distinguish legal/constitutional validity from sociological acceptance and political performance. Explain that foreign recognition is a separate external dimension; treat the listed factors as possible influences, not an exhaustive universal test.

open_items.detail: The source gives Jean Bodin's dates as 1530–1596 and attributes a modern theory of sovereignty to him. Scholarly reference dates him 1529/30–1596 and identifies The Six Books of the Commonwealth (1576) as his major sovereignty work.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, use the precise date range 1529/30–1596 (noting 1530 as a common rounded form), identify the 1576 work, and accurately attribute Bodin's historical definition as absolute and perpetual power of a commonwealth. Explain its period context rather than presenting it as current universal law.

open_items.detail: The characteristics section says a sovereign state 'receives order from none' and that its powers cannot be limited. This is a classical doctrinal position, not an uncontested description of modern international law.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, distinguish Bodin's historical doctrine from contemporary international law. Explain sovereign equality and good-faith Charter obligations under UN Charter Article 2(1)–(2); do not teach sovereignty as exemption from all international obligations.

open_items.detail: The source defines de facto sovereignty by acquisition through force and de jure sovereignty by acquisition under domestic law. Modern scholarship distinguishes factual/effective control from normative/legal status; these are not simply two methods of acquisition.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, define de facto in terms of actual control and de jure in terms of legal entitlement/status or recognition; explain that control and legal status may diverge. Also distinguish internal/external dimensions from legal/political perspectives, and avoid defining internal authority as applying only to nationals.

open_items.detail: The source states that democracy is 'the best form of government'. This is a normative evaluation, not an objective settled fact; scholarship records both broad support and continuing disagreement about democracy's justification and institutional forms.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, attribute the claim to proponents or to the source's viewpoint, present major arguments and criticisms neutrally, and distinguish empirical claims about democratic performance from normative arguments about desirability.

open_items.detail: The source's features list uses 'one man, one vote' and emphasizes majority rule without explicitly explaining minority-rights protection and constitutional limits.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, use inclusive 'one person, one vote' language and explain that majority decision-making operates within constitutional rights, rule of law and protections for minorities. Keep this as a normative/institutional explanation, not a claim that every country meets the ideal.

open_items.detail: The source generalises that democracy in an 'illiterate society' is dangerous and that elections produce violence and malpractice. These are not universal facts and the literacy claim risks stigmatizing whole populations.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, present these as attributed criticisms or context-dependent risks, avoid stereotyping people by literacy, and distinguish possible electoral malpractice from the defining features of democracy. Do not reproduce sensational or graphic detail.

open_items.detail: The Week Four reading pointer cites Essential Government (C.C. Dibie), pages 9–16, and Comprehensive Government (J.U. Anyaele), pages 11–13 and 15–18. Exact editions were not supplied or opened.

open_items.detail: The communalism section presents collective land ownership, absence of private property/classes and barter as universal features. African land-tenure research describes varied and overlapping communal, individual and other rights; the textbook list is an idealized model, not a uniform African or current Nigerian legal order.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T1-W05-CORRECTED-WEEK, explicitly label communalism as a political/economic model or ideal type. Explain that communal land tenure varies and can coexist with individual rights and other tenure arrangements; do not generalize one model to all communities or present it as current law.

open_items.detail: The source calls feudalism a uniform 'primitive system of government' practised in Western Europe in the Middle Ages and describes kings granting fiefs to subjects. Scholarship treats 'feudalism' as a contested retrospective term with varied meanings and regionally different institutions.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, define the narrow feudo-vassalic use of the term, describe the Western European medieval context without implying uniformity, and explain fiefs and lord-vassal obligations as historically varied arrangements. Attribute the historiographical debate and avoid presenting every vassal as a king's subject.

open_items.detail: The source uses 'serf' and 'vassal' as if they were interchangeable. Historical scholarship distinguishes peasant servile status from the lord-vassal relationship, which often involved members of the landed elite.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, define serf/villein and vassal separately. Explain that serfdom is not simply slavery or ordinary paid service, and that vassalage is not synonymous with serfdom. Cite a dated medieval-history source.

open_items.detail: The source says industrialisation brought about the collapse of feudalism. The decline of serfdom in England is documented from roughly 1300–1500, before the Industrial Revolution, and scholarship identifies multiple economic, demographic, legal and social causes.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, replace the single-cause industrialisation claim with a dated, region-specific account. Distinguish the decline of serfdom from the broader and contested transition from feudal institutions to capitalist economies; do not imply one simultaneous European endpoint.

open_items.detail: The source claims feudalism laid the foundation for capitalism and uniformly created order/security. These are debated historical interpretations, not settled universal benefits.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, attribute these as arguments made by some accounts, explain the context and limits, and avoid a simple inevitable progression from feudalism to capitalism. Cite dated historical scholarship.

open_items.detail: The source presents constant war, insecurity and absence of national government as universal features of feudalism. These varied by period and place and should not be generalized to all medieval Western Europe.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, frame these as criticisms or features documented in particular contexts; distinguish decentralized authority from the claim that no national government existed everywhere. Avoid sensational or graphic detail.

open_items.detail: The Week Five reading pointer cites Essential Government (C.C. Dibie), pages 18 and 25–26, and Comprehensive Government (J.U. Anyaele), pages 23–24. Exact editions were not supplied or opened.

open_items.detail: The source defines socialism mainly as government ownership of production and attributes the formulation of socialism to Karl Marx. Socialist thought and movements predate Marx; the term gained currency in the early nineteenth century among several distinct movements.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T1-W06-CORRECTED-WEEK, distinguish socialism as a broad family of ideas from state-socialist models. Note that Marx was an influential theorist, not the originator of all socialism; distinguish socialism from social democracy and other mixed-economy arrangements. Attribute features that apply only to particular models.

open_items.detail: The source gives Karl Marx's dates as 1816–1883. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy records 1818–1883.
open_items.required_action: Correct the date to 1818–1883 and cite the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Do not imply Marx originated all socialist thought; cite pre-Marxian socialist movements.

open_items.detail: The source states that no country has ever practiced communism, while describing communism as state ownership of everything. Scholarship distinguishes historical communist-party states and state-socialist models from the theoretical stateless, classless communist ideal.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, distinguish communist-party governments and historical state-socialist systems from the theoretical classless/stateless ideal. Attribute the source's absolute claim and explain the distinction; do not present state ownership as the full theoretical definition.

open_items.detail: The source says capitalism emerged after the fall of socialism 'in the 1900s', treats minimal government as a defining feature and closely associates capitalism with democracy. Capitalism predates the twentieth century; capitalist economies can be regulated/mixed and can exist under democratic or authoritarian political regimes.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, correct the chronology; distinguish laissez-faire capitalism from regulated/mixed capitalist economies; distinguish economic systems from political regimes; and explain that the late-twentieth-century collapse or transformation of some state-socialist systems did not mean socialism disappeared everywhere. Do not claim capitalism is inherently democratic.

open_items.detail: The class list at lines 510–517 has broken numbering and conflates peasants, wage workers and marginal groups. It also describes the comprador bourgeoisie using a moralized/criminal stereotype rather than its political-economic meaning.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, define bourgeoisie and proletariat by their relationship to ownership and wage labour; distinguish peasants from wage workers; treat lumpenproletariat as a contested historical term, not all unemployed people or a security category; define national and comprador bourgeoisie as analytical categories concerning domestic accumulation and relations with foreign capital. Do not label individuals or groups as criminal based on class terminology. Preserve the original numbering defect in the source record.

open_items.detail: The Week Six reading pointer cites Essential Government (C.C. Dibie), pages 18–24, and Comprehensive Government (J.U. Anyaele), pages 19–22. Exact editions were not supplied or opened.
open_items.required_action: Obtain and inspect the exact editions before confirming the cited pages or relying on their content. Do not reproduce unavailable textbook pages.

open_items.detail: Week Six contains 15 exercises across evaluation, general evaluation, weekend assignment and theory blocks, but the source provides no answer key, marks or marking criteria.
open_items.required_action: GOV-LES-T1-W06-CORRECTED-WEEK must include complete original keyed practice with criterion-level marks that sum exactly and account for all 15 source exercises. Keep contested ideological questions neutral and distinguish definitions from evaluations.

open_items.detail: The source says Italian Fascism began in 1922 and ended in 1943. The movement was founded in 1919; Mussolini came to power in 1922 and was deposed in 1943; a German-backed Fascist successor regime continued in northern Italy until 1945.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T1-W07-CORRECTED-WEEK, distinguish the 1919 movement foundation, 1922 accession to government, Mussolini's 1943 removal and the successor regime's 1943–1945 period. Do not collapse these into one date range.

open_items.detail: The source generalizes that fascism rejects religion and both capitalism and socialism. Italian Fascism's relationship with religion and the economy was more complex; the Lateran Treaties were signed with the Catholic Church in 1929, and private property and business remained under the regime.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, present fascism as a historically varied ideological family. Qualify claims about religion and capitalism using the Italian case; distinguish anti-Marxist/anti-liberal rhetoric from the actual institutions and alliances of the regime. Attribute generalizations rather than stating them as universal facts.

open_items.detail: The 1933–1945 dates for Nazi rule in Germany are accurate. The racial-superiority statement at line 579 is the Nazis' false racist ideology, not a fact about any human group.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T1-W07-CORRECTED-WEEK, state the 1933–1945 dates, identify racial superiority as a false racist belief promoted by the Nazi regime, and explain that race is not a biological hierarchy. Attribute the ideology and reject its claim; do not reproduce propaganda or graphic detail.

open_items.detail: The source says totalitarianism is also called authoritarianism. Political-science literature distinguishes the concepts: authoritarianism is broader, while totalitarianism is generally used for more ideologically driven regimes seeking pervasive control. The boundary is debated.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, define totalitarianism and authoritarianism separately, explain their relationship and the scholarly debate, and avoid using them as synonyms.

open_items.detail: The source's language about absolute control over every person, idea and property is too literal. Totalitarianism is an analytical concept/ideal type describing an ambition for pervasive ideological and institutional control, not proof of perfect control.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, describe totalitarian features as regime aims and institutional patterns, not literal omnipotence. Distinguish documented features from analytical generalizations and avoid sensational or graphic examples.

open_items.detail: The Week Seven reading pointer cites Essential Government (C.C. Dibie), pages 26–28, and Comprehensive Government (J.U. Anyaele), pages 22–23. Exact editions were not supplied or opened.
open_items.required_action: Obtain and inspect the exact editions before confirming the cited pages or relying on their content. Do not reproduce unavailable textbook pages.

open_items.detail: Week Seven contains 15 exercise items across the mid-week evaluation, evaluation questions, general evaluation, weekend assignment and theory blocks. The source provides no answer key, marks or marking criteria.
open_items.required_action: GOV-LES-T1-W07-CORRECTED-WEEK must include complete original keyed practice with criterion-level marks that sum exactly and account for all 15 source exercises. Treat the mid-week block at line 574 as an assessment, not a week boundary; explicitly note that three weekend questions assess earlier topics.

open_items.detail: The source lists recognition, membership/citizenship and law as separate essential state characteristics. The Montevideo Convention Article 1 identifies permanent population, defined territory, government and capacity to enter relations; Article 3 states political existence is independent of recognition by other states.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T1-W08-CORRECTED-WEEK, distinguish the common textbook characteristics from the Montevideo Convention criteria. Explain that recognition is important in practice but not a constitutive requirement under the declaratory approach; citizenship and a written constitution are not separate Article 1 criteria. Qualify 'free from external control' as independence, not isolation from international obligations.

open_items.detail: The source says a state cannot cease to exist unless conquered in war. International law recognizes dissolution, merger/unification, separation and other forms of state succession; conquest is not the only route.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, distinguish continuity of a state through changes of government from the possibility of state dissolution or merger. Use dated examples such as the Soviet Union and Czechoslovakia; do not imply that conquest is required for state extinction.

open_items.detail: The source states that a nation possesses all attributes of a state except sovereignty. Scholarship distinguishes nations from states and ethnic groups; nations may exist without sovereign statehood, while states may contain multiple national communities.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, distinguish nation, state and nation-state. Define a nation as a political community formed through shared identity, history, public culture and mutual commitment/self-understanding; avoid defining it as a state with one missing attribute or requiring common descent.

open_items.detail: The source says Nigeria's federal structure and political beliefs, values and attitudes were copied from Britain. British colonial administrative and constitutional policies influenced the system, but Nigeria's federal arrangement emerged through colonial constitutional reforms and Nigerian political negotiations; the Lyttleton Constitution of 1954 formally introduced the federal system.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, give a dated account of the 1953–1954 constitutional conferences and Lyttleton Constitution. Explain colonial administrative influence alongside the role of Nigerian nationalist and regional actors; do not say Nigeria simply copied Britain's own federal model.

open_items.detail: The source's determinants section describes ethnicity as fixed 'tribal' cultures and characterizes urban/developed populations as more educated/participatory and rural populations as conservative. These are overgeneralizations and risk treating group identity as deterministic.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, present ethnicity, historical experience, socio-economic conditions and political instability as possible contextual influences, not fixed predictors. Avoid stereotyping rural/urban populations or assuming all members of an ethnic group share one political culture. Retain the cognitive, affective and evaluative components accurately.

open_items.detail: The Week Eight reading pointer cites Essential Government (C.C. Dibie), pages 4–6 and 16–17, and Comprehensive Government (J.U. Anyaele), pages 8–9. Exact editions were not supplied or opened.
open_items.required_action: Obtain and inspect the exact editions before confirming the cited pages or relying on their content. Do not reproduce unavailable textbook pages.

open_items.detail: Week Eight contains 13 exercise items across evaluation, general evaluation, weekend assignment and theory blocks, but the source provides no answer key, marks or marking criteria.

open_items.detail: The source defines political socialization as educating citizens and transmitting political culture across generations. Political socialization is broader and lifelong: it begins in childhood, continues in adulthood, and includes informal as well as formal learning.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T1-W09-CORRECTED-WEEK, define political socialization as a lifelong process through which people acquire, reinforce and sometimes revise political orientations. Include formal and informal learning and avoid restricting it to adult citizens or classroom education.

open_items.detail: The source generalizes that politics and religion always go together and that religious groups direct members toward a political course. Religious groups may influence public debate and political socialization, but their roles vary and members' political choices are not uniform. Nigeria's Constitution s.10 prohibits adoption of a state religion; ss.38, 40 and 42 protect religious freedom, association and non-discrimination.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, describe religious organizations as one possible agent of political socialization, not a universal or compulsory political authority. Distinguish religious participation in public debate from state religion; explain members' freedom of conscience and association. Use the Constitution and present differing positions neutrally without naming or stereotyping faith communities.

open_items.detail: The Week Nine reading pointer cites Essential Government (C.C. Dibie), pages 17–18, and Comprehensive Government (J.U. Anyaele), pages 14–15. Exact editions were not supplied or opened.

open_items.required_action: GOV-LES-T1-W09-CORRECTED-WEEK must include complete original keyed practice with criterion-level marks that sum exactly and account for all 11 source exercises, including the cross-week state item. Resolve the political-socialization and religion distinctions above.

open_items.detail: The source lists the UK, France and Italy as unitary states. This classification is broadly correct, but the UK has extensive devolution; France and Italy have written constitutions and regional autonomy.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T1-W10-CORRECTED-WEEK, retain the examples but qualify them: explain that unitary status concerns the constitutional source of ultimate authority, not the absence of local government or devolution. Use dated official constitutional/parliamentary sources.

open_items.detail: The source says unitary constitutions are flexible and parliament is supreme. These features apply to the UK constitutional tradition but not to all unitary states: France and Italy have written constitutions with formal amendment procedures and constitutional review.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, distinguish the UK's parliamentary sovereignty/uncodified constitution from France's Article 89 and Italy's Article 138 amendment procedures. Do not define unitary government by constitutional flexibility or parliamentary supremacy.

open_items.detail: The source lists Nigeria, the United States, India and Russia as federal states. Their constitutions support federal classification, but the distribution of powers and degree of centralization differ.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, cite Nigeria Constitution s.2(2), the U.S. Constitution's federal/state allocation, India's Union-of-States framework and Russia Constitution arts.1 and 5. Note that formal federal status does not mean identical autonomy or practice.

open_items.detail: The source presents small/large size and homogeneous/heterogeneous populations as if they determine the suitability of unitary or federal government, and presents advantages/disadvantages as guaranteed outcomes.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, frame size, diversity, efficiency, minority protection and administrative cost as arguments and possible trade-offs, not necessary rules or guaranteed results. Explain that institutional design and political practice matter.

Explain the principle, its constitutional scope and implementation without inventing or attributing the definition to the source. Include a keyed practice item.

open_items.detail: The source describes the Berlin Conference (1884–1885) as the event that partitioned West Africa. The German Federal Foreign Office states that the conference established rules for European territorial claims and trade/navigation; it did not draw specific borders. It was hosted by Bismarck and ran from 15 November 1884 to 26 February 1885.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T2-W01-CORRECTED-WEEK, give the accurate dates and distinguish the conference's framework for claims from the subsequent, uneven process of conquest, treaties and boundary-making. Attribute the conference's colonial purpose; do not teach that it drew all West African borders.

open_items.detail: The source says 1885–1950s was the period of colonial rule in West Africa. Independence dates varied; UN records include Nigeria (1960), Sierra Leone (1961), The Gambia (1965), Guinea-Bissau (1974) and Cabo Verde (1975).
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, avoid a single 1950s end-date. Use a small dated selection of country examples to show the different decolonization timelines across West Africa.

open_items.detail: The source dates the Industrial Revolution to the seventeenth century. Britannica dates the first Industrial Revolution in Britain broadly to the eighteenth century, often 1760–1840.
open_items.required_action: Correct the date to the eighteenth century (with c.1760–1840 as a common periodization) and explain that industrialization was one economic context for European expansion, not the sole cause of colonialism.

open_items.detail: The source says Europeans introduced slavery to maintain colonies and describes bringing culture/religion as bringing civilization. Slavery existed in Africa before European arrival; the transatlantic slave trade predated formal colonial administrations. The 'civilizing mission' was a colonial justification, not an objective fact.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, distinguish the earlier histories of slavery and the transatlantic slave trade from later colonial labour systems. Present 'civilizing' claims as colonial ideology/justification, and frame economic, strategic, missionary and political motives as varied by empire and territory.

open_items.detail: The source attributes the introduction of indirect rule to 'Sir Lord Lugard' and says it followed success in India and Uganda. Scholarship describes Lugard's role in developing and applying indirect rule in Northern Nigeria and emphasizes adaptation to existing local institutions and regional circumstances; the model was not unique to Britain.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, describe Lugard's role specifically in Northern Nigeria and explain how British administrators adapted indirect rule to existing political systems. Do not claim that one individual introduced a uniform system throughout Nigeria or that India and Uganda were identical models.

open_items.detail: The source gives lack of staff, cost, language and climate as reasons for indirect rule, and says it was introduced merely to preserve customs. These explanations need qualification; indirect rule also served colonial control, taxation and administration, and its effects varied.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, present staffing, cost, language and existing institutions as factors rather than a complete or single-cause explanation. Qualify the disease/climate claim and explain that preservation of custom was not the sole or neutral purpose of colonial rule.

open_items.detail: The source says traditional rulers were members of legislative councils as a general feature of indirect rule. Roles differed by region and period; Native Authorities and legislative councils were distinct institutions.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, distinguish Native Authorities, local administration and legislative/advisory councils. Qualify tax collection, law/order and representation as roles that varied by location and period.

open_items.detail: The source generalizes that Islam taught political submissiveness and that low literacy among Northern Nigerians caused indirect rule to succeed. These are unsupported, stereotyping claims. Existing emirate and Native Authority structures were important in some areas, but Northern Nigeria was not institutionally uniform.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, remove the religious and literacy stereotypes. Explain the varied precolonial political institutions, including emirate systems in some areas, colonial administrative choices, taxation and local responses/resistance. Do not attribute a single political attitude to a religion or population.

open_items.detail: The scheme at preamble children 13–14 says indirect rule in Northern, Western and Southern Nigeria. Week One body children 75–80 cover Northern Nigeria; Week Two body child 91 covers Western Nigeria and child 102 explicitly says Eastern Nigeria. The scheme's 'South' and the body's 'East' are not silently interchangeable.
open_items.required_action: Preserve the exact scheme and body wording at their separate locators. Do not harmonize 'South' to 'East' without owner/teacher decision or authoritative source comparison; a later correction may clarify the intended regional scope.

open_items.detail: Week Two body children 127–139 do teach positive and negative impacts of colonial rule in West Africa, so the scheme objective is not missing from the combined Week One/Two span. However, the claims about elections, banking/currency, slave-trade chronology, leader deportations, language antagonism and industrial development need factual correction or qualification.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T2-W02-CORRECTED-WEEK, provide a balanced and evidence-based account of the positive and negative impacts, correct the dated examples and distinguish colonial institutions from pre-existing African systems. Do not treat this objective as absent; keep its coverage PARTIAL until corrections are delivered.

open_items.detail: The EVALUATION marker at body child 82 is followed only by a reading pointer, workbook pointer and past-WASSCE-paper pointer at children 83–85. No explicit question stems, marks or answer key appear in the Week One span.
open_items.required_action: Record this as a marker and do not invent source questions, answers or marks. If the teacher expects a specific evaluation set, obtain the missing original questions; any new formative practice must be clearly labelled original.

open_items.detail: The Week One reading pointer names J.D. Fage, A Short History of Africa, with a Penguin Books imprint but no edition, year, chapter or page range. The workbook and past WASSCE papers are not identified or attached.
open_items.required_action: Obtain the exact Fage edition and assigned pages/chapter, and identify the workbook and WASSCE paper/year/question numbers before treating these as verifiable assignments. Do not reproduce unavailable book or examination content.

open_items.detail: The source describes Yoruba political institutions through the Alaafin of Oyo and says the majority of Yorubas were Christians, with Christianity less conservative than Islam. The Oyo example is not representative of all Yoruba polities, and religious communities cannot be reduced to a single political temperament.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T2-W02-CORRECTED-WEEK, explain the Oyo example with its checks on the Alaafin (including the Oyo Mesi) while noting regional variation. Remove the Christianity/Islam stereotype; describe Yoruba religious life as diverse and do not treat religious affiliation as a deterministic cause of political behaviour.

open_items.detail: The source says Eastern Nigeria lacked traditional rulers/chiefs and describes all Igbo political systems as decentralized, egalitarian and gerontocratic. Scholarship emphasizes substantial diversity: many communities were decentralized, while some (including Onitsha, Oguta and Umueri) had monarchic institutions.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, distinguish the absence of a single centralized kingship in many communities from the absence of political institutions. Explain village councils, age grades, associations and local variation; do not describe all Igbo communities as institutionally identical.

open_items.detail: The source links the 1929 Aba Women's War directly to the failure of indirect rule. Historical accounts identify multiple causes, including taxation, fears of extending taxation to women, warrant chiefs, native courts, market grievances and colonial administrative practices. The protest was not a single-cause event.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, use the historically grounded term Women's War/Rebellion (1929) and explain its varied causes and political agency. Do not reduce it to a simple proof that indirect rule failed everywhere in Eastern Nigeria or describe it as only a 'riot'.

open_items.detail: The source credits the indirect-rule system with ending twin infanticide through Mary Slessor. Mary Slessor was a Scottish Presbyterian missionary who arrived in Calabar in 1876 and died in 1915; she opposed the killing of twins in some communities. Her missionary work is not an outcome of indirect rule and should not be conflated with colonial administrative policy.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, distinguish Mary Slessor's missionary activity from the indirect-rule system. Attribute her documented work accurately, avoid the claim that indirect rule itself ended the practice, and acknowledge local families and community actors rather than using a colonial-saviour narrative.

open_items.detail: The source presents the merits and demerits of indirect rule as universal outcomes: low cost, preservation of traditions, training of rulers, autocracy, elite alienation and divide-and-rule. The outcomes varied by region and colonial administrative practice; indirect rule could preserve, alter or create local authorities.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, present these as context-dependent effects, distinguish traditional rulers from appointed warrant chiefs and Native Authorities, and explain that local institutions were often reshaped under colonial control. Avoid treating every ruler or community as identical.

open_items.detail: The source dates the West African Currency Board and first silver coins to 1912 and says a 'Colonial Bank' was established in 1917. The West African Currency Board was established in 1912 and began issuing currency in 1913; the Bank of British West Africa was founded in 1894. The source's 1917 institution name/date is not supported as written and needs exact identification.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, distinguish the West African Currency Board from commercial banks, give the 1912 establishment/1913 currency-issue dates, and identify the bank intended by the source before retaining any 1917 date. Do not invent a replacement bank name.

open_items.detail: The source credits colonialism with introducing modern government, elections, civil service, parties and education as if these were sole or uniformly positive colonial creations. The 1922 Clifford Constitution introduced a limited elective principle in Nigeria, with the first elections in 1923 and representation restricted to Lagos and Calabar; colonial institutions also interacted with pre-existing African political systems and initiatives.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, give dated, specific examples and qualify colonial institutional changes. Distinguish the limited 1922 elective principle from universal suffrage, identify the 1923 elections and the NNDP's 1923 formation where relevant, and avoid presenting colonialism as the sole source of political development.

open_items.detail: The source says Oba Ovonramwen was exiled in 1896 after the Benin events and that Jaja of Opobo died in the West Indies. Ovonramwen was exiled to Calabar after the British punitive expedition of 1897 and died in 1914. Jaja was exiled to the West Indies and died on the return journey at Tenerife in 1891.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, distinguish the two events: the 1897 British punitive expedition and Ovonramwen's exile/death; Jaja's 1887 deportation, later permission to return and death en route at Tenerife in 1891. Use neutral historical wording and no graphic detail.

open_items.detail: The source describes English- and French-speaking West African states as antagonistic and says this is one of ECOWAS's problems. ECOWAS was established in 1975 and works across English, French and Portuguese official languages; language differences can create coordination challenges but do not make antagonism inevitable.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, explain colonial language legacies as one factor in regional relations while acknowledging multilingual cooperation and ECOWAS's integration mandate. Qualify claims about cultural imperialism and economic dependence as historical arguments supported by evidence, not universal statements about every territory.

open_items.detail: The source states that industries were not built in West Africa. Colonial economies were often organized around export production and limited industrial diversification, but the absolute claim that no industries existed is too broad; development varied by territory and sector.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, describe export-oriented colonial economic structures and limited industrialization without saying no industries existed. Attribute the broader dependency thesis to its scholarly source and use specific evidence.

open_items.detail: The scheme at preamble children 13–14 says indirect rule in Northern, Western and Southern Nigeria. Week One body children 75–80 cover Northern Nigeria; Week Two body child 91 covers Western Nigeria and child 102 explicitly says Eastern Nigeria. The scheme's 'South' and the body's 'East' are not silently interchangeable.
open_items.required_action: Preserve the exact scheme and body wording at their separate locators. Do not harmonize 'South' to 'East' without owner/teacher decision or authoritative source comparison; a later correction may clarify the intended regional scope.

open_items.detail: The EVALUATION marker at body child 141 is followed only by a workbook practice pointer at child 142. No explicit question stems, marks or answer key appear in the Week Two span.
open_items.required_action: Record this as a marker and do not invent source questions, answers or marks. If the teacher expects a specific evaluation set, obtain the missing original questions; any new formative practice must be clearly labelled original.

open_items.detail: The Week Two source points to an unnamed workbook for further practice; no edition, exercise numbers or pages are supplied.
open_items.required_action: Obtain the exact workbook edition and assigned exercise numbers before treating this as a verifiable practice assignment. Do not reproduce unavailable workbook material.

open_items.detail: The source lists education as a positive impact. University College Ibadan was established in 1948 as a college of the University of London and became an independent university in 1962. Formal colonial education expanded, but it did not originate all education in West Africa; Islamic, mission, indigenous and other educational traditions predated or coexisted with it.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T2-W03-CORRECTED-WEEK, state the University College Ibadan chronology accurately and distinguish colonial formal schooling from pre-existing and parallel educational traditions. Avoid presenting colonialism as the sole origin of education or knowledge.

open_items.detail: The source says West African economies were introduced to the world economy when Africans were 'not ready'. This is paternalistic and ignores extensive precolonial local, regional and long-distance trade and diplomatic networks.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, explain that colonial rule reoriented and intensified particular export relationships; do not suggest West Africa had no prior trade, diplomacy or economic networks. Use evidence and avoid the phrase 'not ready'.

open_items.detail: The source discusses colonial condemnation of African ways of life and the portrayal of African cultures as inferior. This should be attributed to colonial racial/cultural ideology, not treated as a factual description of African societies.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, explain cultural hierarchy as an ideology used to justify colonial domination, while presenting African societies as diverse and historically complex. Attribute claims and avoid repeating colonial stereotypes as facts.

open_items.detail: The source claims colonial rule neglected rural areas and developed urban centres. This may describe patterns in particular territories, but the statement is too broad without specific evidence, dates and examples.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, qualify the claim and support it with a specific territory/period and evidence about transport, public investment, services or export infrastructure. Do not state it as a universal outcome.

open_items.detail: The six-row table treats British indirect rule and French assimilation/direct administration as mutually exclusive, uniform systems. Michael Crowder notes that both systems could use chiefs, although their roles differed; later scholarship also finds regional variation and the importance of local intermediaries in French West Africa.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, distinguish indirect rule, direct administration, assimilation and association. Explain differences without claiming that French authorities never used chiefs/customary institutions or that British practice was always indirect. The table's visual layout remains assigned to GOV-VIS-T2.

open_items.detail: The source gives a single list of governor functions for 'West Africa'. British West African colonies had different constitutions and legislative arrangements; the governor's powers varied by colony and period.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, identify the specific colony and constitutional instrument for each power (e.g. assent, emergency powers, prerogative of mercy and reporting). Do not generalize one colony's constitutional arrangements to all British West Africa.

open_items.detail: The source attributes a definition of nationalism to K.B.C. Onwubiko but provides no edition or page. Its formulation links nationalism to common language and common historical experience, which is too narrow for multi-ethnic and multilingual nationalist movements; the phrase introducing the quotation is also grammatically corrupted.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T2-W04-CORRECTED-WEEK, give a concise original definition centered on collective political identity/self-determination and opposition to foreign rule. Explain that common language/history may contribute but are not required. Verify the Onwubiko attribution against the exact edition/page before retaining it.

open_items.detail: The source says the First World War caused the world economic depression. The Great Depression began in 1929; post-World War I economic and financial instability contributed to the conditions, but the two events are not the same and the relationship is not a simple one-step cause.
open_items.required_action: Separate wartime/postwar economic hardship from the Great Depression of the 1930s. Explain the 1929 onset and describe how global economic shocks affected colonial economies and nationalist sentiment without asserting a single cause.

open_items.detail: The source lists Jimi Solanke alongside Kwame Nkrumah, W.E.B. Du Bois and Nigerian nationalists. Reliable biographies identify Jimi Solanke primarily as an actor, poet, storyteller and cultural artist; his inclusion as a nationalist political leader is unsupported. W.E.B. Du Bois is more accurately identified as a Pan-Africanist intellectual/organizer, not a Nigerian nationalist leader.
open_items.required_action: Do not guess which name the source intended. Remove or separately classify Jimi Solanke unless a specific nationalist role can be evidenced. Distinguish Du Bois's Pan-Africanist contribution from the work of Nigerian nationalist party leaders.

open_items.detail: The source says nationalism led to rapid economic growth in West Africa and 'sold West Africa to the outside world by being popular'. The first is an unsupported causal generalization; the second is unclear and cannot be interpreted confidently.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, retain well-supported effects such as political mobilization, party formation, labour organization, political education and independence. Do not claim rapid economic growth without evidence; ask the source owner/teacher to clarify the unclear phrase or leave it uncorrected in the source record.

open_items.detail: The source lists West African Pilot, Lagos Weekly Record, Lagos Daily News and Sierra Leone Weekly News and abbreviates NNDP, CPP, NCNC and AG without dates or distinct national contexts. The NNDP was founded in 1923; the NCNC in 1944; the CPP in 1949; the Action Group in 1951. These parties were not all Nigerian or led by the same people.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, name each party in full, identify its territory and founding date, and connect each to the correct leaders. Distinguish the newspapers' publication histories and avoid presenting West African nationalism as a single Nigerian organization.

open_items.detail: The source credits Pa Michael Imoudu with making unions undertake a nationwide strike. Imoudu was a prominent labour leader and mobilizer, but the 1945 general strike was organized through trade unions and a joint labour leadership; he should not be represented as its sole organizer.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, describe Imoudu's role in labour mobilization and the 1945 general strike with reference to the unions' collective organization and the workers' demands. Avoid attributing the whole action to one person.

open_items.detail: The source says Macaulay resisted a British law that put all lands in Southern Nigeria under British control and says he co-founded the Daily News. Historical accounts describe his protests over land issues and a 1922 land case involving a Lagos chief; he and Dr John Caulcrick bought the Lagos Daily News in 1927, while the paper had been founded in 1925. The source's blanket land-law description and 'co-founded' wording need correction.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, identify the exact ordinance or land case and avoid claiming it placed all Southern Nigerian land under British control unless primary evidence supports that. Distinguish the newspaper's 1925 founding from Macaulay/Caulcrick's 1927 purchase. Retain the verified NNDP founding date of 1923.

open_items.detail: The source gives Azikiwe's birth and political offices broadly correctly, but the West African Pilot was founded in 1937 (the source's '1937–1940' period is unsupported), and while NCNC was founded in 1944, Azikiwe became its Secretary-General in 1946 according to historical biographies.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, use the verified dates: born 16 November 1904; founded the West African Pilot in 1937; co-founded NCNC in 1944 and became its Secretary-General in 1946; Premier of Eastern Region 1954–1959; Governor-General 1960–1963; President 1963–1966.

open_items.detail: The source gives Ahmadu Bello's birth year as 1909. Oxford's Dictionary of National Biography dates his life 1910–1966 and identifies him as Premier of Northern Nigeria. The NPC emerged as a cultural association before becoming a political party in 1951.
open_items.required_action: Correct the birth year to 1910 and distinguish the NPC's earlier cultural-association history from its emergence as a political party in 1951. Verify any specific schools attributed to Bello before listing them.

open_items.detail: The source says Awolowo co-founded the Trade Union Congress in 1943. Historical accounts show the TUC of Nigeria emerged in 1943 and that Awolowo was involved in labour organizations and served as editor of the Nigerian Worker, but the source does not establish that he was a co-founder. His Western Region premiership (1954–1959) and 1955 free-primary-education programme are well supported.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, distinguish Awolowo's labour involvement from the formal founding leadership of the TUC. Retain the verified 1954–1959 premiership and 1955 free primary education policy with dated sources.

open_items.detail: The source names 'Nana of Itsekiri' and 'Awujale of Ijebu land' without identifying the individuals or events. The Itsekiri figure is Nana Olomu, captured and exiled to the Gold Coast in 1894. Awujale is a royal title, not a personal name; the source does not identify which officeholder/event. Jaja and Ovonramwen's exile chronology is already documented in the Week Two open items.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, identify Nana Olomu and give the 1894 context. Specify the Awujale by personal name and date/event only if supported by a reliable historical source. Cross-reference the Week Two Jaja/Ovonramwen corrections; do not duplicate or alter those source records.

open_items.detail: The 1922 Order in Council specifies the Governor as President, 26 official members, 15 nominated unofficial members and four elected unofficial members: three for Lagos and one for Calabar. The source says three elected members represented Calabar, which is incorrect, and calls officials 'white' rather than identifying them as colonial officers.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T2-W05-CORRECTED-CONSTITUTIONS, reproduce the correct composition and allocation. Explain that the Legislative Council's jurisdiction was confined to the Southern Provinces (including Lagos); the Governor legislated for the North by proclamation. Do not state that the elective principle was first in Africa; it was introduced in Nigeria by this constitution.

open_items.detail: The source says the Clifford Constitution established a new executive council for the whole country. A national Executive Council already existed before 1922; the major 1922 change was the new Legislative Council replacing the Nigerian Council, while the Executive Council remained an official colonial body without Nigerian members.
open_items.required_action: Correct the distinction between the pre-existing Executive Council and the 1922 Legislative Council. Do not attribute the creation of the Executive Council to the Clifford Constitution.

open_items.detail: The source attributes the emergence of NNDP, NYM and NCNC, and newspapers such as Lagos Daily News and West African Pilot, to the 1922 constitution. The NNDP followed in 1923, but the NYM (1934), NCNC (1944), Lagos Daily News (1925) and West African Pilot (1937) came later and were not created by the 1922 constitution.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, say the elective principle stimulated later political activity, but give each party and newspaper its own date and context. Cross-reference the Week Four press/party open item; do not imply the 1922 constitution directly created organizations founded years later.

open_items.detail: The Richards Constitution came into operation on 1 January 1947, created a central Legislative Council and regional councils/assemblies, and retained a restricted elective franchise. The regional councils were consultative/advisory, not independent regional legislatures; the Richards-era income threshold for the limited Lagos/Calabar franchise was reduced to £50. Its stated aim of promoting unity must be distinguished from its regional structure and later political effects.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, distinguish the central Legislative Council from regional councils, give the operational date, explain the £50 threshold and restricted franchise, and separate the constitution's stated aims from later assessments of regionalism and political division.

open_items.detail: The source describes the Macpherson Constitution's regional structures, 12-member Council of Ministers and different regional voting arrangements. The broad structure is supportable: Northern and Western legislatures were bicameral, the Eastern legislature unicameral, and the Council of Ministers had four members from each region. The source's claim of full regional autonomy is overstated; the Action Group's 1951 formation should not be presented as a result of the constitution.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, explain the 1951 constitutional structure precisely, distinguish regional powers from full sovereignty, and present the Action Group's formation as a separate contemporaneous political development. Specify that the North's franchise was restricted to male taxpayers while women could vote in the East and West under the relevant regional arrangements.

open_items.detail: The source dates Anthony Enahoro's motion for self-government in 1956 to 1 April 1953. The motion was moved on 31 March 1953. The subsequent 1953 Kano crisis contributed to the breakdown of political cooperation and constitutional negotiations; the Macpherson Constitution was replaced by the Lyttleton Constitution in 1954, not instantaneously on the day of the riots.
open_items.required_action: Correct the motion date to 31 March 1953 and describe the 1953 crisis as a process leading to constitutional breakdown and the 1954 Lyttleton settlement. Keep the historical account non-graphic and avoid reducing the crisis to one cause.

open_items.detail: The scheme coverage record preserves the exact scheme wording 'Clifford constitution of 1992', while the assigned source is headed 'Clifford Constitution of 1922'. This appears to be a scheme typo, but the scheme text must not be silently rewritten during source indexing.
open_items.required_action: Keep the original scheme wording and the source heading at separate locators. Record the likely year correction in the factual follow-up and obtain owner/teacher confirmation before altering the scheme itself.

open_items.detail: The scheme asks for the features, objectives, merits and demerits of each pre-independence constitution. The Week Five source gives features, merits and demerits for Clifford, Richards and Macpherson but does not provide a clearly separated, evidence-based statement of each constitution's stated objectives.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, identify each constitution's stated aims from the relevant historical instruments/official records and distinguish those aims from later merits/demerits. Do not invent objectives from retrospective claims.
